articles.title: Residential Proxy Infiltration Exposes Compromised White House Networks
articles.content: Our Residential Proxy Observatory , launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity. While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650 . AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network. Confirmed residential proxy activity observed from the White House network, October 5 to November 3, 2026. What we observed From October 5 to November 3: Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network 236 separate times . Those exits came from 6 addresses , on 26 of the 30 days . 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network. To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits. This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services. Why this is concerning Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them. Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets , the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems. No place is too remote The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet. Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena. We also recorded three observations from Antarctica . All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station. Other remote places with activity: Pitcairn : 1 Starlink address, 1 observation. Norfolk Island : 1 Norfolk Telecom address, 4 observations. Svalbard : 1 Starlink address in Longyearbyen, 3 observations. Also seen: the Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7). Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide. For relevant agencies: We have backed up the raw logs of the recorded activity and are willing to share them. You can request them through our contact page .

articles.title: United Nations Reshapes World Court Bench Amid Record Geopolitical Lawsuits
articles.content: xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoJudges arrive at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to hear South Africa's request on a Gaza ceasefire in The Hague, the Netherlands, on May 24, 2024 [File: Nick Gammon/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff4 Nov 2026The United Nations has elected five judges to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for nine-year terms, as the court faces a record caseload, including South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza. The vote was held on Tuesday at UN headquarters, with candidates requiring an absolute majority in both the General Assembly and the Security Council to win. Dapo Akande of the United Kingdom, Francois Alabrune of France, Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud of Jordan, Rena Lee of Singapore and Phoebe Okowa of Kenya were elected to the 15-member panel. The two UN bodies initially agreed on four candidates but failed to select a fifth. The Security Council supported Ecuador’s Marcelo Vazquez-Bermudez, while the General Assembly backed Okowa, prompting further rounds of voting. Vazquez-Bermudez later withdrew from the race, and Okowa subsequently won the backing of the General Assembly and the Security Council. The votes were held by secret ballot concurrently, but separately. The ICJ is based in The Hague and has 15 judges, each from a different country. They serve nine-year terms and may be re-elected. To ensure a degree of continuity, a third of the bench is elected every three years. The election comes as the World Court faces a record workload. ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa told the General Assembly on October 29 that 24 contentious cases are pending, covering disputes over territory, human rights and the interpretation of international treaties. Among them is South Africa’s case accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in its war on Gaza. The court has previously ordered provisional measures but has not issued a final ruling on whether genocide occurred. In October 2025, the court issued an advisory opinion outlining Israel’s obligations towards the UN and humanitarian organisations operating in the occupied Palestinian territory. Separately, the court announced on Tuesday that it would deliver a judgment on November 19 in The Gambia’s case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya minority. Established in 1945, the ICJ is the UN’s principal judicial organ, responsible for settling disputes between states and providing advisory opinions on questions of international law.

articles.content: Firms still want kit on-premises, but spike in revenue is as much about increased costs as higher sales Dan Robinson Dan Robinson IT INFRASTRUCTURE REPORTER Published wed 4 Nov 2026 // 17:30 UTC Make us preferred on Google Meta brings Conductor on board its model train now Windows pushed AI PCs, but now it's hit a wall of RAM prices 14 hours ago Datacenter operators must win hearts and minds, not just permits 15 hours ago Drax wants to feed Britain's AI habit with £20B datacenter at biomass power station 1 day ago Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B 2 days ago On-premises high-performance compute (HPC) is still in demand, according to Hyperion Research, which estimates the market is expanding at almost 20 percent year-on-year, often driven by requirements for AI processing. What Hyperion calls the "on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science" server market showed significant growth in the first half of 2026, with revenues hitting $16.5 billion, up 19.9 percent. However, the analyst says unit shipments over the same period grew only 4.4 percent, meaning that systems are carrying a higher price tag due to greater use of costly components such as GPUs and other accelerators, not to mention the effects of higher memory costs, which have tripled or quadrupled since last year. Its tracking of the HPC market is based on multiple surveys conducted of both buyers and suppliers, the firm says. The latest data shows a major change in the overall HPC market growth, heavily driven by a combination of the use of AI, large language models (LLMs), and purchases of large GPU/accelerator-based systems. This trend was noted a couple of years ago, with Omdia reporting in 2024 that revenue growth from server sales was racing ahead of actual units shipped, as customers prioritized investment in highly configured server clusters for AI . Much of that spending was by hyperscalers and cloud providers, seeking to profit from selling AI services to enterprise customers, but Hyperion’s figures focus on on-prem shipments, showing that many enterprises prefer to do their processing in-house. According to Hyperion, Dell has now surpassed HPE as the biggest HPC vendor, with server revenues of $4.2 billion for the first half of 2026. HPE, which picked up supercomputing specialist Cray for $1.3 billion in 2019, had long been pack leader in the global HPC arena in terms of market share and revenue. The figures put Dell on a 24 percent share, while HPE is not far behind on 21 percent. Lenovo and China-based Sugon trail behind at 4 percent share each, while 45 percent of the market is just labelled as "others" by Hyperion. This includes names such as Bull, which re-emerged from the shadows of Atos this year, plus Supermicro, Penguin Computing, and NEC. The HPC infrastructure market is inherently cyclical. HPE recognized significant revenue in 2025 with sales of multiple exascale-class leadership machines, but procurement of that scale is intermittent and doesn't necessarily come along every year, Hyperion notes.  "Organizations and institutions are continuing to invest in their advanced computing infrastructure due to both replacing aging machines and the desire to adopt AI into their workflows to support their businesses and missions," said Hyperion Research CEO Earl Joseph. "The growth reflects both a nominal increase in units being purchased and significant increases in system prices." HPC systems are considered the backbone for many AI and AI-related applications, which has driven the overall HPC market to a new growth level, Joseph added. ® ai on-prem server hpc supercomputing month 2026 Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: South African Electoral Commission Tightens Security After Ballot Sabotage
articles.content: Ballot storage facilities have been targeted, election materials damaged and arrests made across several provinces, leaving thousands of police and the IEC racing to secure the voting process ahead of Wednesday’s polls. By Reitumetse Pilane and Nonkululeko Njilo 3 Nov 2026 0 Inside the National Results Operations Centre at Gallagher Convention Centre, where political parties, independent candidates and media will monitor the polls during the 2026 Local Government Elections. (Photo: Reitumetse Pilane) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper Hours before millions of South Africans head to the polls, the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has been forced to beef up security at ballot storage facilities across KwaZulu-Natal following a series of disruptions, including an incident in which party supporters stormed a facility and prevented election officials from carrying out their duties. The most serious incident occurred on Monday evening, 2 November, at the Dassenhoek Library Satellite Warehouse in Marianhill, west of Durban, where a group wearing political party clothing entered the premises and demanded that ballot boxes containing special votes be moved elsewhere, claiming the building was not secure because it had previously been broken into. The facility serves 24 voting stations in the area, and the confrontation disrupted operations at two of them after election officials were prevented from moving freely in and out of the premises to collect election material. Similar attempts to gain access to ballot storage facilities were reported in Richmond, Mkhambathini and Pietermaritzburg, although police managed to prevent those involved from entering, prompting the IEC to request additional security across the province. Speaking to journalists at the KwaZulu-Natal results centre in Durban on Tuesday, the IEC’s provincial electoral officer, Ntombifuthi Masinga, said: “We have now requested that the SAPS reinforce security in all our storage facilities in the province.” IEC chief executive Sy Mamabolo addresses media at the National Results Operations Centre at Gallagher Convention Centre in Midrand, Johannesburg on 2 November 2026. (Photo: Reitumetse Pilane) During a separate national briefing in Midrand, Gauteng, IEC chief executive Sy Mamabolo identified those involved in the Marianhill incident as alleged uMkhonto Wesizwe (MK) party supporters and said election officials had been held hostage before police intervened. “Public order police were called in to disperse these supporters and secure the officials and the election materials. Fortunately, the group left peacefully after engagement with the SAPS,” Mamabolo said. However, the MK party’s Willies Mchunu cast doubt on suggestions that those involved were party members and condemned the incident in the strongest possible terms. IEC investigates political party involvement While Mamabolo had identified those involved as alleged MK party supporters, the provincial IEC said it was still investigating whether the people wearing party clothing were genuine members or individuals pretending to represent the party. Responding to a question from Daily Maverick, the commission said it could not yet confirm their political affiliation and was working to establish who had entered the premises before taking legal action. “All the people that were in that precinct were wearing party apparel. Masinga said the people had claimed to belong to a party, “but we cannot unfortunately say with certainty” that this had been the case. The commission said it had already approached the political party concerned and was examining video footage of the incident to determine whether those involved were party members or people pretending to represent the party. “We have engaged the political party concerned, and we will be able to ascertain whether those were their members or people who were pretending to be, or people who were masquerading as, members of a political party,” the IEC said. The commission made it clear that those responsible would face legal consequences once the investigation had established their identities. “We will definitely press criminal charges,” Masinga said.  KZN leads in high-risk voting stations The incidents come against the backdrop of heightened election security in KwaZulu-Natal, where 165 voting stations have been identified as high risk, the highest number in the country. More than 10,000 police officers have reportedly been deployed ahead of the Wednesday, 4 November local government elections. National Police Commissioner Fannie Masemola. (Photo: Gallo Images / Frennie Shivambu) Last week, National Police Commissioner Fannie Masemola revealed that more than 300 voting stations across the country had been identified as high-risk, with KwaZulu-Natal accounting for nearly half of them. Speaking in Durban on Friday, Masemola said police had identified areas where protests, political tensions and other security-related incidents could affect voting, with most of the province’s high-risk stations concentrated in eThekwini. “These voting stations are located in areas potentially to experience either instability, particularly, be it your protests and/or other security-related incidents,” he said. “KwaZulu-Natal has the highest number of those voting stations. We have identified 165 across the province, of which 124 are in eThekwini, and the others are distributed around uThukela, 16, 13 in Amajuba, 11 in Zululand and one in Ugu.” Gauteng has also been identified as a province of concern, with provincial police commissioner Tommy Mthombeni confirming that 119 voting stations had been classified as high-risk. IEC defends security arrangements Despite the incidents, the IEC has defended the security arrangements at its ballot storage facilities, saying the initial police deployments were considered sufficient because officials had not anticipated groups forcing their way on to the premises. “I wouldn’t necessarily say that the SAPS was not prepared. I think the numbers that they had posted in these facilities were adequate in a normal circumstance,” the IEC said during Tuesday's provincial briefing. “But no one would have predicted that in one out of so many, there [would] be people forcing their way into the precinct.” The commission explained that the Marianhill facility presented a particular challenge because it shared an entrance with a public library, making it difficult for security personnel to distinguish people visiting the library from those attempting to gain access to the ballot storage area. Although police eventually dispersed the group, the IEC acknowledged that reinforcements had not arrived as quickly as it would have liked, but maintained that officers had managed to restore order and secure the election material. “It may not be as quick as we would have loved to see it happening, but they got reinforcement, and those people were driven out of the facility,” the commission said. The IEC also revealed that some political parties had demanded permission to deploy their own private security companies at storage facilities, despite the presence of permanent security personnel, SAPS officers and private security guards appointed by the commission. “They also want to post their own private security companies, and we did not allow that,” the IEC said, explaining that it believed the existing arrangements were sufficient. “Three layers of security, as far as we are concerned, are sufficient to secure these storage facilities.” Other election-related incidents The IEC has also reported incidents involving election officials and political party candidates in other parts of the country, raising further concerns about attempts to interfere with election operations. Masinga confirmed that a presiding officer in Hammarsdale, KwaZulu-Natal, had been suspended after arranging for her son to collect her from a voting station in a vehicle branded in ANC colours, while she was in possession of election material. In the Eastern Cape, two individuals allegedly posed as IEC officials and attempted to collect election material from the eNgcobo Police Station, but were prevented from gaining access. “These two failed to access the materials. They were positively identified as members of Ngcobo Yethu Civic Organisation. One of the impersonators is a PR Councillor candidate for the same party and has since been arrested by the SAPS,” Mamabolo said. In Mpumalanga, a councillor candidate for Ward 30 in the Phake Rankaila voting district was arrested after allegedly storming a voting station and damaging election material. The commission condemned the incidents and said it was taking legal steps to hold those involved accountable. “The above conduct cannot be justified nor allowed to impair the country’s electoral process. Therefore, the commission is taking the necessary legal steps to bring the identified individuals and political parties to account,” the IEC said. Police on high alert Police are on high alert across the country for Wednesday’s local government elections, with the National Joint Operational and Intelligence Structure (NatJoints) warning that intimidation, violence and attempts to disrupt voting will not be tolerated. Deputy National Police Commissioner Lieutenant General Tebello Mosikili said 21 election-related cases had been recorded across the country since Sunday, 1 November 2026. (Photo: Gallo Images / OJ Koloti) Speaking during a briefing on Tuesday evening, Lieutenant-General Tebello Mosikili said security forces had stepped up their preparations to ensure that voters could cast their ballots safely, particularly in areas identified as potential hotspots for election-related violence and unrest. Mosikili said 21 election-related cases had been recorded across the country since Sunday, including murder, intimidation, arson, theft and damage to election materials, with six dockets resulting in arrests and five cases already processed in court. She also confirmed that police were investigating the killing of an MK party regional leader in KwaZulu-Natal, with support from political killing task teams. “We recognise that these incidents have caused concern, particularly as the country approaches election day. However, we wish to assure South Africans that every incident brought to the attention of our operational structures is receiving the necessary attention and that appropriate interventions are being implemented,” she said. Tuesday, 3 November, marked the final day of special voting ahead of the local government elections, with the process catering for registered voters who may be unable to visit their voting stations on election day because of illness, physical impairments or work and travel commitments. With voting set to take place nationwide on Wednesday, 4 November, authorities have urged South Africans to exercise their democratic rights peacefully and allow the electoral process to proceed without interference. articles.title: UK Supreme Court Tests Boundaries of Digital Activism Bans
articles.content: Clara LALANNE Nov 3, 2026 Add AL-MONITOR on Google More than 20 protestors supporting Palestine Action were arrested by police outside the court — Henry NICHOLLS Britain's highest court on Wednesday heard an appeal against a government ban on activist group Palestine Action, proscribed as a terrorist organisation, as police arrested protestors gathered outside. The two-day hearing at the Supreme Court comes as the ban has failed to quell support for the pro-Palestinian group co-founded by Huda Ammori, leading to mass arrests across the UK. "I urge the Supreme Court justices to bring this authoritarian overreach—and the chilling censorship it has unleashed—to an end once and for all," Ammori said in a statement. Multiple protesters carrying signs supporting Palestine Action -- prohibited under terrorism laws -- were arrested by police on Wednesday. More than 300 supporters were detained at protests at the weekend. UK-Brazilian actor Alfred Enoch told AFP he was demonstrating Wednesday against the ban because it "has a chilling effect on people's ability to engage democratically in one of the great issues of their time, which is the struggle for emancipation of the Palestinian people." Protestor Yael Kahn said she joined Wednesday's demos because people "have been arrested, just for the words" written on a placard. According to campaign group Defend Our Juries, which has organised demonstrations backing the movement, around 4,200 people have been arrested since the British government outlawed Palestine Action in July last year. Those detained include large numbers of pensioners, among them a priest, a former financial adviser, a military veteran and Swedish student climate activist Greta Thunberg. Public support for Palestine Action is a criminal offence as the ban places the group in the same legal category as the Islamist Al-Qaeda organisation and Lebanon's Iran-backed Hezbollah. The ban followed a series of acts of vandalism linked to the movement, including a trail of damage at a Royal Air Force base and actions targeting Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems in August 2024. It was imposed under the UK's Terrorism Act and made membership of or support for the pro-Palestinian group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Ammori's lawyer Raza Husain told the court that out of 385 actions undertaken by the group in the last five years, "only three passed the terrorism threshold". "Palestine Action fall within the tradition of a direct action protest group motivated by conscience," Husain said. The group has "never advocated for violence against the persons", she added. In February, London's High Court dealt a blow to the government, ruling the decision to proscribe Palestine Action was "disproportionate". The court found the ban had resulted in "substantial interference" with the rights of freedom of expression and assembly. However, the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in June, concluding the ban was "not unlawful" and that Palestine Action was "a covert organisation operating with secret cells". The appeal ruling added that it was "a fundamental mistake to overlook the fact that Palestine Action overtly promotes unlawful violence amounting to terrorism". - 'Direct action' - Founded in 2020, Palestine Action describes itself as "a direct action movement committed to ending global support for Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime". The organisation gained prominence after the outbreak of the Gaza war, triggered by Hamas's unprecedented attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. Ammori has been granted permission to challenge the ban at the UK's highest court on a narrow procedural ground, arguing the Home Office failed to follow its own criteria in its decision. If unsuccessful, Ammori has indicated she will take the case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). The Home Office is set to reject the characterisation of the group as "non-violent", according to court documents.  Prominent Jewish groups also said in written submissions supporting the government that the Jewish community was "especially vulnerable to Palestine Action's violent activities". ctx-cla/jkb/ach  This one's on us. articles.title: Apple Delays Critical Siri API Integrations Leaving Developers Stranded
articles.content: More than two years after promising it, Apple lets developers test Siri AI app integration Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published wed 4 Nov 2026 // 20:56 UTC Make us preferred on Google Apple turns iCloud into spy cloud, will start looking at public share links 2 hours ago Nvidia is happy to take your money whether you're using open or closed models, says Jensen Huang 1 day ago Apple's Mac business is booming, but the memory market has other plans 1 day ago Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights 1 day ago AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes 2 days ago As of Tuesday, developers can explore expanded Siri AI integration for their Apple platform apps through beta releases of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Next spring, nearly three years after announcing plans for deeper third-party Siri integration, Apple expects to begin accepting App Store submissions using the new capabilities. "This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers," Apple said in a developer news post . "With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers."  Anything is likely to be an improvement. Apple's Siri, a voice-activated assistant service, dates back to 2011 and gained limited third-party app access in 2016. In 2024, it became an interface for interacting with Apple Intelligence, its suite of generative AI features. Apple Intelligence has not been very intelligent – several advertised Siri capabilities were delayed, so much so that Apple was sued in 2025 over allegations of misleading marketing. After a shakeup of Apple's machine learning group in December 2025, Siri and Apple Intelligence received a makeover at Apple's Worldwide Developers Conference in June. "Before this year, Siri was a timer with a voice," said Roberto Gutierrez, Apple platforms staff engineer at a media company and author of the e-book On-Device Intelligence, in an email to The Register . "Weather, alarms, calls. Anything past that was a coin toss.  "On the developer side, SiriKit covered a handful of domains and Shortcuts only worked if users memorized the phrase. Siri AI is the first version that understands context and can chain actions across apps. That's a real change." There is a catch, however, Gutierrez observed. Siri AI is available in a limited number of languages and regions. Support for Traditional Chinese is expected by the end of 2026, and EU availability remains a matter of negotiation – Siri AI is unavailable on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS in the bloc as Apple works through interoperability concerns under Europe's Digital Markets Act. "Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward," the company said last month without committing to any concessions. Gutierrez said that he expects opening Siri to third-party developers will be useful to some extent. "Siri can only do what apps expose through App Intents, and SiriKit is on its way out," he said. "If your app's main actions aren't exposed, the new Siri can't see you. The bigger shift is letting Claude, Gemini and others plug in. Developers already choose between three options for every AI feature: Apple's system model, an open model through MLX, or a cloud API. Siri is heading the same way. It doesn't need to be the smartest model. It needs to be the best router. That's the right call." Apple has made choosing between those three options more difficult by failing to publish benchmarks that show how its Foundation Models compare with open-weight alternatives. The biz has published measurements of how its third-generation Foundation Models compare to their 2025 predecessors. But the company's commitment – to "[share] more details on our latest foundation models, including updated evaluations and benchmarks, in a technical report later this summer" – remains unfulfilled so far as we're aware. Gutierrez ran  his own benchmark s to compare Apple's iOS system model (FM system, ~3B) to several open-weight models that are suitable for use on-device. "On an A17 Pro iPhone running iOS 26, I tested Apple's system model against Qwen3 1.7B and 4B, Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 3 4B on a structured-output task," he said. "Speed: Apple's model ran at about 149 tok/s, roughly 3x the fastest open model (Qwen3 1.7B, about 46)." Quality, he said, was a tie, with every model passing five typed checks. But memory, he said, was where Apple's models had an advantage. "The system model's weights live outside your app's memory budget," he explained. "My app peaked at 12 MB during inference. An open 4B model costs 2.4-2.7 GB, and a 2.4 GB model plus your app plus a WebView is a crash report. So yes, it's competitive, and on iPhone it's the default I'd recommend. If you want your own model, Qwen3 1.7B is the one." But Gutierrez urged Apple to publish proper competitive benchmarks. "Their numbers compare against their own previous models," he said. "Developers aren't choosing between Apple 2025 and Apple 2026. We're choosing between Apple, Qwen and a cloud API. I had to build my own harness to answer a question Apple could settle with one table." The absence of competitive model metrics is not the only gap. Apple has also failed to accommodate web apps. "Web apps are locked out," said Gutierrez. "Foundation Models is a Swift API (and now Python). No JavaScript, no WebKit. A PWA's only option is to ship its own model into the browser and pay the full memory bill inside a WebView." And bringing your own model may pose performance problems. "On an A17 Pro iPhone, the 3-4B open models pushed the phone into 'fair' thermal state and dropped to 12-24 tok/s," he said. "In practice, your own model on iPhone means ~2B or smaller." With Siri AI unavailable on iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches in the EU (and its rollout in mainland China subject to regulatory requirements), developers may need a fallback for global apps to handle regional restrictions. Apple's Private Cloud Compute offers eligible developers access to Foundation Models, Gutierrez observed, though it requires membership in the App Store Small Business Program, fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads across their apps, and the necessary entitlement. ® ai and ml siri apple intelligence artificial intelligence apple app store Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Moldova Defeats Russian Hybrid Cyber Sabotage During Accession
articles.content: The European Commission has held up Moldova as an example for other EU-aspirant states to follow, both in terms of internal reforms and resilience to Russian interference, while also praising Albania, Montenegro, and Ukraine. Enlargement commissioner Marta Kos told press in Brussels, on Wednesday (4 November) that, out of the four frontrunners, Albania, Moldova, and Montenegro were “on track” for EU accession by 2030, despite anti-government riots in Tirana this year. But she added that Moldova was “the best performer” showing “strong determination” to implement reforms. Albania started EU accession talks in 2022, Montenegro in 2012, while Moldova and Ukraine began theirs in 2024. The EU has long praised Kyiv for advancing reforms while at the same time fighting off Russia’s war machine. But Chișinău’s progress also took place against a backdrop of growing hybrid attacks from Russia, such as drones entering the country’s airspace, cyberattacks , and Moldovan citizens recruited to perform sabotage. It has also been forced to deal with disinformation campaigns originating from Moscow and the buying of an estimated 100,000 votes in its 2024 presidential elections in favour of an anti-EU candidate. “For the first time, we have opponents who are interfering in our accession process,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU foreign affairs chief, speaking alongside Kos on Wednesday. Moldova has collaborated with EU countries to push back against Russian interference and its experiences also helped “refine the EU’s toolbox for countering hybrid threats,” according to a commission progress report on its enlargement progress out on Wednesday. But despite these efforts, hackers still gained access to citizens’ personal data from government databases on Tuesday (3 November). The prime minister, Vasile Tofan, suspects the attack was run by a state actor. Russian military forces have also controlled the Transnistria region in eastern Moldova since 1992, but this would “not become an obstacle” to the country’s EU admission, Kallas told Moldova’s prime minister in May. For its part, Ukraine also hopes to join the EU by 2028, but the commission said this was an "ambitious" target, given the size of the country. Michael Gahler, a German centre-right MEP dealing with Ukraine, told EUobserver the 2028 was “achievable”, if “necessary reforms continue at pace”. But he added that it was yet to open EU talks on integrating its massive agricultural sector into the single market, which would be “one of the most complex chapters in Ukraine's accession negotiations.” Meanwhile, accession talks with Georgia, Serbia, and Turkey had been de facto frozen due to democratic backsliding, the commission reports noted. But in Serbia, where the opposition won parliamentary elections on 25 October, it was “time for a fresh start,” Kos said. Talks with Bosnia and North Macedonia were also limping along due to internal political divisions in Sarajevo and North Macedonia's bilateral dispute with Bulgaria over languages and history, with little sign of progress in either file. When candidate countries wrap up their EU negotiations, each of the 27 member states still need to ratify their accession, in a final hurdle. And in France, where anti-immigrant and anti-enlargement feeling was on the rise, this meant either a referendum or a three-fifths supermajority in a parliament vote. Unlock article and share

articles.title: Canva Restructuring Accelerates Contagion Across Australian Tech Capital
articles.content: Advertisement Dunja Popovs woke up on Wednesday to the news that she was one of the 22 per cent of design software maker Canva’s workers losing their job . “Truthfully, I am sad and devastated, but I’m also extremely grateful that I ever had the opportunity in the first place,” Popovs, who led a team of content designers at Canva, wrote on LinkedIn. Her plan for now is “a whole lot of gardening”, then to start hunting for a new job. Cliff Obrecht, Melanie Perkins and Cameron Adams at the Canva Create conference in Los Angeles in April. Canva chief executive Melanie Perkins told staff on Wednesday that 1271 people would be affected by a restructuring, aimed at resetting the business after growth started to slow this year. Advertisement Some will lose their jobs. Others will be asked to relocate or will find their roles rewritten. The timing was brutal: the news arrived a day after the Reserve Bank lifted rates to an 18-year-high. Anyone who has tried to get hired in tech knows not much happens between now and Australia Day. The news took me back to April, when I saw Canva close its biggest product launch ever in a Los Angeles football stadium with engineers in gold plastic crowns playing Ode to Joy on instruments that included a rubber duck. I asked co-founder Cliff Obrecht the question every Australian tech boss was getting that month. Atlassian, WiseTech and Telstra were cutting thousands of jobs, much of it put down to AI. Was Canva next? The answer was definitive. “We do not have to do layoffs, and we don’t have any plans to do layoffs,” Obrecht said. Canva’s headcount growth had slowed from 50 per cent a year to under 5 per cent, and he pitched that as the grown-up alternative to what everyone else was doing. “Rather than this gas-on, hit-reverse, lay-off kind of mentality,” he said, “we’ve seen this coming, and we’ve just eased our foot off the accelerator.” Advertisement I believed him, and so did plenty of the people who got the email on Wednesday. One departing engineer described it as the “grim reaper of the tech world” arriving “a lot sooner than I thought it ever would”. Most staff were surprised, he said. To be fair to Obrecht, I think he meant every word. Canva had been profitable for nine straight years and had more than $US1.5 billion ($2.2 billion) in the bank. It had never needed to do major layoffs. Then the numbers turned , in large part due to the rapid rise of AI. In August, I reported that Canva had slowed that product launch because AI bills were eating its margins. Canva co-founder Cliff Obrecht. Peter Rae “Historically, the cost to create a design cost us essentially nothing,” Obrecht said in August. “The cost of goods to serve a user has gone from cents per month to many, many more cents.” Advertisement Canva’s internal valuation of its business, used to price staff shares, tumbled as a result, and Perkins’ email confirmed growth slowed this year for the first time in a decade. She didn’t link the cuts directly to AI, but others are less sure the threat is temporary. Adam Barty, who runs Melbourne AI agency Revium, says it’s “pretty hard not to view AI as an existential threat to Canva’s core business model”, which is to give people who aren’t designers an easy way to make things free and convert enough of them into paying subscribers. Some long-term users have moved their slideshows and social posts to AI chatbots and barely open Canva anymore. For a decade, Canva has been the most successful story in Australian tech: a 19-year-old in Perth and her boyfriend, more than 100 investor rejections, then the most valuable start-up this country has produced. Its co-founders are now billionaires and every pitch deck in Surry Hills borrowed a little of its shine. Canva’s Cliff Orbrecht (left), Cameron Adams and Melanie Perkins. Getty Advertisement This setback is grim news for staff, but also for Australia’s venture capital sector, which has effectively been propped up by Canva’s outsized success. Venture capital firm Blackbird owns about 10 per cent of Canva, and it has been a huge success for the firm until now. Airtree first invested in 2014 and has asked its own investors to keep its fund open until 2028 in the hope of a payday. Behind both firms sit wealthy families, endowments and super funds. If Canva’s value keeps sliding, so does the case that backing Australian start-ups is a sound use of retirement savings. Where things go from here is an open question, as is Canva’s very survival over the long term. An IPO looks further off than ever. A sale to a global tech giant near Canva’s current value could be an option and would be one of the biggest software deals ever done. Advertisement But there’s always a silver lining. When Google shut its Wave project (an attempt to build a social media platform for users to collaborate) in Sydney in 2010, a crop of talented engineers went looking for something new. One of them was Cameron Adams, who became Canva’s third co-founder. Canva is about to release a much bigger crop, with $US10,000 grants for anyone who wants to start their own business. If even a handful of those are successful, then Australian tech’s next big story started on Wednesday. David Swan travelled to Los Angeles in April with the support of Canva.
